source: Cambodia National IPM Program (MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension), in cooperation with FAO — "Cabbage Integrated Pest Management: An Ecological Guide" (adapted from J.W. Ketelaar & A.L.M. Abubakar), August 2008, 266 pages, Chapter 1 sections 1.1-1.2
text:
Integrated Pest Management (IPM, វិធានការចម្រុះគ្រប់គ្រងដំណាំ) is described as closely tied to crop pest control but going beyond it to focus on the whole production system and market outcomes, not just eliminating pests. IPM does not aim to wipe out every pest in a field; some pest presence is actually necessary to sustain the natural enemies (predators and parasitoids) that keep pest populations in check. The goal of IPM is to keep pest numbers below the level that would cause real yield loss, rather than pursuing pest-free fields. Early IPM programs concentrated mainly on reducing pesticide use, but the guiding principle broadened into building farmers' clear understanding of the crop's own ecosystem -- including the natural relationships between pests, natural enemies, and other factors in and around the field -- through regular field observation as the basis for management decisions.

Field experience applying IPM on vegetable crops has shown that production can be managed to substantially cut spending on pesticides (including herbicides) without reducing yield; in fact, yields tend to rise when IPM practices are followed. One example cited in the source: in Vietnam, among about 140 farmers tracked through farmer field schools from 1996 to 1999, only around 40% of farmers following conventional practice achieved good results and cabbage yields under ordinary practice stayed flat, while farmers who applied IPM achieved yields roughly 64% higher than the conventional farmers' usual yields.

The FAO-IPM Inter-Country Programme on Vegetable Crops in South and Southeast Asia (Phase 1) is identified as a five-year regional program (April 1996 to June 2001) to develop and implement IPM for vegetable production, supported by the Netherlands and Australia, with government and NGO cooperation across Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, Indonesia, Laos, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam. Its aim was to help vegetable production become more profitable while reducing environmental harm, pursued through developing and scaling up IPM training among agricultural staff and farmer alumni.

The program's approach is framed as aiming to 'empower vegetable farmers' -- building farmers' own capacity to make sound crop-management decisions -- through a training curriculum covering: field ecosystem-analysis techniques; techniques for controlled rearing/observation of insects for study purposes; participatory research and extension/communication techniques; and training farmers themselves to become facilitators and community trainers who can pass the knowledge on further. The program's primary training vehicle is the Farmer Field School (FFS), paired with a Training-of-Trainers (TOT) track and a participatory action-research approach (Farmer Research) intended to produce lasting results.
caveat: This source is a 266-page FAO/MAFF IPM manual for cabbage (cabbage Source D); this file covers only sections 1.1-1.2 (pages 1-2 of the source's own pagination). A few individual words in the introductory paragraph were faint on the available scan and have been paraphrased for overall meaning rather than quoted verbatim; the Vietnam case-study figures (140 farmers, 1996-1999, 40%, ~64% yield gain) were legible and are reported as printed.
